metadata.title: A phase transition for the probability of being a maximum among random vectors with general iid coordinates

extraction_notes.note: Remark 2 is only an instance of multiple maxima, so it is retyped as an example. Remark 3 introduces weak maxima and the weak Pareto-front, so it is retyped as a definition. Remark 1 stays a remark.

One sentence both introduces U and asserts p^(U)=p^(F)=q^(F)=q^(U) for continuous F. It is typed as a claim rather than a definition because a node cannot split a sentence; it is the source of the term edges for p^(U).

The proof of Theorem 1 is all of Section 4, in prose, with Lemma 1, a remark and the lemma's proof inside it, plus a starred continuation subsection. It is one proof node, with the lemma block as a setup step. The proof node stops at the closing box, before the Acknowledgement.

For the Bernoulli exact formulas, the derivation is written as the display chain itself (law of total probability, conditioning on the multinomial counts). It cannot be separated from the claimed formula, so no separate proof node was made.

The argument for gamma in (0,1] is interleaved with the separate assertion that gamma=1 for continuous F. It is split into two proof parts (PP2, PP3) that both prove ClP5, with ClP4 as its own claim between them.
The abstract and introduction copies are kept in also_stated_at, although the introduction puts the threshold at gamma*log(n) where Corollary 1 has gamma^{-1}*log(n).

Not extracted: the Figure 1 caption (numerical observations), the introduction's roadmap and literature survey, and Ferguson's Theorem 2. Ferguson's result is only applied inside proof step PSP23, so it gets no node of its own.

nodes.name: Min/max wedge-vee notation
nodes.statement: In addition, in several places of this manuscript we denote the minimum (resp. maximum) of some real numbers $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ by $\underset{i}{\wedge} x_i \equiv \min_i x_i$ (resp. $\underset{i}{\vee} x_i \equiv \max_i x_i$).
nodes.section: 2 Model description and the main result

nodes.name: Product order
nodes.statement: It is based on the product order $\preceq$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$, \textit{i.e.,} for every two vectors $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^k$ such that $a=(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k)$ and $b=(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_k)$ define \begin{equation} a\preceq b\Leftrightarrow \left(a_i\leq b_i\ , \ \forall 1\leq i\leq k\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Coordinatewise (product) partial order $a\preceq b$ iff $a_i\le b_i$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Product order relation
nodes.statement: a\preceq b\Leftrightarrow \left(a_i\leq b_i\ , \ \forall 1\leq i\leq k\right).

nodes.name: Strict product order
nodes.statement: Similarly, define \begin{equation} a\prec b \Leftrightarrow \left( a\preceq b \ and \ \exists i \in [k] \: s.t. \: a_i < b_i \right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Strict product order relation
nodes.statement: a\prec b \Leftrightarrow \left( a\preceq b \ and \ \exists i \in [k] \: s.t. \: a_i < b_i \right).

nodes.name: Maximum (strong) and Pareto-front
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ be $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^k$. In addition, let $\preceq$ be the product order on $\mathbb{R}^k$. Then, for each $1\leq i\leq n$, $x_i$ is a maximum with respect to $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ iff there is no $j\neq i$ such that $x_i\preceq x_j$. In addition, the set of maxima with respect to $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is called the Pareto-front generated by $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$.
differentia: there is no $j\neq i$ such that $x_i\preceq x_j$
nodes.statement_short: $x_i$ is a (strong) maximum if no other $x_j$ weakly dominates it; the set of maxima is the Pareto-front.
also_stated_at: A vector is said to be a (strong) maximum if and only if (iff) there is no other vector in the sample that (weakly) dominates it in all coordinates.
nodes.label: def: maximum

nodes.name: Definition 1 is a strong maximum
nodes.statement: \normalfont Definition \ref{def: maximum} refers to a \textit{strong} maximum. To see this, consider the special case in which $k=1,n\geq2$ and $x_1=x_2=\ldots=x_n$. In this case, $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ are all maxima in the usual sense but none of them is a maximum in the sense of Definition \ref{def: maximum}.
nodes.statement_short: Equal vectors are all usual maxima but none is a maximum in the sense of Definition 1.

nodes.name: Multiple maxima
nodes.statement: \normalfont It is possible to have multiple maxima in the sense of Definition \ref{def: maximum}. For instance, assume that $n=k=2$ and consider the case in which $x_1=(1,0)$ and $x_2=(0,1)$.

nodes.name: Weak maximum and weak Pareto-front
nodes.statement: \normalfont It is natural to introduce another notion of multivariate maximum: $x_i$ is a {\it weak} maximum with respect to $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ iff there is no $j\neq i$ such that $x_i\prec x_j$. Correspondingly, the set of weak maxima with respect to $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is called the \textit{weak} Pareto-front generated by $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$. Later, in Section \ref{subsec: bernoulli} we discuss this notion once the coordinates have a Bernoulli distribution.
differentia: there is no $j\neq i$ such that $x_i\prec x_j$
nodes.label: remark:weak_strong

nodes.name: iid array X_ij
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{X_{ij} ;i,j\geq1\right\}$ be an infinite array of iid real-valued random variables having a distribution function $F$.

nodes.name: Random vectors X_i^k and Pareto index set
nodes.statement: For every $i,k\geq1$ denote $X_i^{k}\equiv\left(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{ik}\right)$ and for every $k,n\geq1$, let $\maxset{k}{n} \subset \{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ be the random set of indices of all vectors that belong to the Pareto-front generated by the random vectors $X_1^k,X_2^k,\ldots,X_n^k$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_i^k$ is the first $k$ coordinates of row $i$; $\mathcal{P}_{k,n}$ is the random set of Pareto-front indices among $n$ vectors.

nodes.name: Event A_{k,n}
nodes.statement: Then, observe that $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1)$ is equal to one iff the event \begin{equation} A_{k,n}\equiv \bigcap\limits_{j=2}^n \overline{\left\{X_1^k\preceq X_j^k\right\}} \: \end{equation} occurs.
nodes.statement_short: Vector 1 is a maximum iff $A_{k,n}$: no other vector weakly dominates it.

nodes.name: Event that vector 1 is a maximum
nodes.statement: A_{k,n}\equiv \bigcap\limits_{j=2}^n \overline{\left\{X_1^k\preceq X_j^k\right\}} \:

nodes.name: Almost-sure convergence via liminf/limsup of A
nodes.statement: Moreover, note that for every sequence $(k_n)_{n\geq1}$ of positive integers, $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}1$ (resp. $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0$) $P$-a.s. iff \begin{equation} P\left(\liminf_{n\to\infty} A_{k_n,n}\right)=1\ \ , \ \ \left[\text{resp. } P\left(\limsup_{n\to\infty} A_{k_n,n}\right)=0\right]. \end{equation}
assumptions: for every  sequence $(k_n)_{n\geq1}$ of positive integers
nodes.statement_short: Indicator of vector 1 being maximal tends to 1 (resp. 0) a.s. iff $P(\liminf A_{k_n,n})=1$ (resp. $P(\limsup A_{k_n,n})=0$).

nodes.name: liminf/limsup criterion
nodes.statement: P\left(\liminf_{n\to\infty} A_{k_n,n}\right)=1\ \ , \ \ \left[\text{resp. } P\left(\limsup_{n\to\infty} A_{k_n,n}\right)=0\right].

nodes.name: Initial observation: fixed k or fixed n
nodes.statement: An initial observation is that: \begin{enumerate} \item For every fixed $k\geq1$, $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0$ , $P$-a.s. \item For every fixed $n\geq1$, $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{k\to\infty}1$ , $P$-a.s. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For fixed $k$ vector 1 is eventually not maximal a.s.; for fixed $n$ it is eventually maximal as $k\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of being a maximum for general k_n
nodes.statement: The main question is how to generalize this observation by characterizing the asymptotic behaviour of $\textbf{1}_{\{\maxset{k_n}{n}\}}(1)$ as $n\to\infty$ for a general sequence $(k_n)_{n=1}^\infty$?
nodes.statement_short: Characterize when vector 1 is eventually a.s. maximal for a general sequence $k_n$.

nodes.name: Random variable X with cdf F
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a random variable with a cumulative distribution function $F$.

nodes.name: Function S (left-continuous survival)
nodes.statement: Define the function $S:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow[0,1]$ as $S(x)\equiv P(X \geq x)$.

nodes.name: Factor gamma
nodes.statement: Next, define \begin{equation} \gamma \equiv \gamma_F \equiv -E\log\left[S(X)\right]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_F=-E\log S(X)$, the functional of $F$ that locates the phase transition.

nodes.name: Definition of gamma
nodes.statement: \gamma \equiv \gamma_F \equiv -E\log\left[S(X)\right].
nodes.label: eq:gamma_def

nodes.name: Phase transition for being a maximum (a.s.)
nodes.statement: Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers \begin{description} \item[(a)] If \begin{equation} \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}>\gamma^{-1}\,, \end{equation} then \begin{equation} \textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}1\, \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} \item[(b)] If \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}< \gamma^{-1}\,, \end{equation} then \begin{equation} \textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0, \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} \end{description}
assumptions: Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers
nodes.statement_short: If $k_n/\log n$ eventually exceeds $1/\gamma$, vector 1 is a.s. eventually a maximum; if it stays below $1/\gamma$, a.s. eventually not.
nodes.label: thm: main result1

nodes.name: Condition (a): liminf k_n/log n > 1/gamma
nodes.statement: \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}>\gamma^{-1}\,,
nodes.label: eq: condition1

nodes.name: Conclusion (a)
nodes.statement: \textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}1\, \ \ P\text{-a.s.}

nodes.name: Condition (b): limsup k_n/log n < 1/gamma
nodes.statement: \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}< \gamma^{-1}\,,
nodes.label: eq: condition2

nodes.name: Conclusion (b)
nodes.statement: \textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0, \ \ P\text{-a.s.}

nodes.name: Probability p_{k,n} of being a maximum
nodes.statement: For every $k,n\geq1$, denote \begin{equation} p_{k,n}\equiv P\left(A_{k,n}\right)=E\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1). \end{equation}
also_stated_at: Let $p_{k,n}$ be the probability that the first vector is a maximum.

nodes.name: p_{k,n} as expectation
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}\equiv P\left(A_{k,n}\right)=E\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1).
nodes.label: eq:p_k_n_def

nodes.name: Corollary 1 via bounded convergence
nodes.statement: Then, an application of bounded convergence theorem yields the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the bounded convergence theorem to the a.s. limits of Theorem 1.

nodes.name: Phase transition for p_{k,n}
nodes.statement: Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers. \begin{description} \item[(a')] \begin{equation} \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}>\gamma^{-1} \Rightarrow \lim_{n \to \infty} p_{k_n,n} = 1. \end{equation} \item[(b')] \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{k_n}{\log(n)}<\gamma^{-1} \Rightarrow \lim_{n \to \infty} p_{k_n,n} = 0. \end{equation} \end{description}
assumptions: Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers.
nodes.statement_short: $p_{k_n,n}\to1$ if $\liminf k_n/\log n>1/\gamma$ and $\to0$ if $\limsup k_n/\log n<1/\gamma$.
also_stated_at: The main result of the present paper is that if $k\equiv k_n$ grows at a slower (faster) rate than a certain factor of $\log(n)$, then $p_{k,n} \rightarrow 0$ (resp. $p_{k,n}\rightarrow1$) as $n\to\infty$.

Namely, we will show that if $k\equiv k_n$ grows at a slower (resp. faster) rate than $\gamma \log(n)$, then $p_{k,n}\rightarrow0$ (resp. $p_{k,n}\rightarrow1$) as $n\to\infty$, where $\gamma \in (0,1]$ is a certain constant that depends on the distribution $F$.
nodes.label: cor: main corollary

nodes.name: Part (a') implication
nodes.statement: \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}>\gamma^{-1} \Rightarrow \lim_{n \to \infty} p_{k_n,n} = 1.
nodes.label: eq: condition first part

nodes.name: Part (b') implication
nodes.statement: \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{k_n}{\log(n)}<\gamma^{-1} \Rightarrow \lim_{n \to \infty} p_{k_n,n} = 0.
nodes.label: eq: condition second part

nodes.name: Generalized inverse S^{-1}
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} S^{-1}(y)\equiv\inf\left\{x\in\mathbb{R};S(x)\leq y\right\}\ \ , \ \ y\in(0,1). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Generalized inverse of S
nodes.statement: S^{-1}(y)\equiv\inf\left\{x\in\mathbb{R};S(x)\leq y\right\}\ \ , \ \ y\in(0,1).

nodes.name: S(S^{-1}(y)) <= y
nodes.statement: Since $S$ is a nonincreasing leftcontinuous function, $S\left[S^{-1}(y)\right]\leq y$ for every $y\in(0,1)$.

nodes.name: gamma = 1 for continuous F
nodes.statement: When $F$ is continuous, the last inequality above holds with equality and $\gamma=1$.
conclusions: the last inequality above holds with equality and $\gamma=1$

nodes.name: gamma = 0 only if S = 1
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\gamma=0$ if and only if $S\equiv1$, which means that $X$ is infinite.
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma=0$ forces $S\equiv1$, impossible for a real-valued $X$.

nodes.name: gamma lies in (0,1]
nodes.statement: Thus, the assumption that $X$ is real-valued implies that $\gamma\in(0,1]$.

nodes.name: gamma for the Bernoulli distribution
nodes.statement: For example, when the coordinates have a $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ distribution for some $p\in(0,1)$, \begin{equation} S(x)=\begin{dcases} 1, & x \leq 0, \\ p, & 0 < x \leq 1,\\ 0, & 1 < x. \\ \end{dcases} \end{equation} Therefore, \begin{equation} \gamma= - p \log(S(1)) - (1-p)\log(S(0)) = - p \log(p) \end{equation} and hence $\gamma=e^{-1} \approx 0.368$ is the maximal value of $\gamma$ for the Bernoulli case, obtained at $p = e^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: For Bernoulli($p$), $\gamma=-p\log p$, maximal value $e^{-1}$ at $p=e^{-1}$.

nodes.name: S for Bernoulli(p)
nodes.statement: S(x)=\begin{dcases} 1, & x \leq 0, \\ p, & 0 < x \leq 1,\\ 0, & 1 < x. \\ \end{dcases}

nodes.name: gamma = -p log p for Bernoulli
nodes.statement: \gamma= - p \log(S(1)) - (1-p)\log(S(0)) = - p \log(p)

nodes.name: F-indexed Pareto set and probability
nodes.statement: We specify the dependence on $F$ explicitly, denoting $\maxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$ the (random) maximal set and $p_{k,n}^{(F)}$ the probability of being a maxima when $X_{ij} \sim F$.

nodes.name: Weak Pareto set and probability q_{k,n}
nodes.statement: Similarly, we denote by $\weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$ the weak Pareto-front generated by $X_1^k,..,X_n^k$ (see Remark \ref{remark:weak_strong}), and define \begin{equation} q_{k,n}^{(F)}\equiv P\left(1\in\weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}\right)=E\textbf{1}_{\weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}}(1). \end{equation}

nodes.name: q_{k,n} as expectation
nodes.statement: q_{k,n}^{(F)}\equiv P\left(1\in\weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}\right)=E\textbf{1}_{\weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}}(1).

nodes.name: Strong maxima are weak maxima
nodes.statement: By definition $X_j^k \succ X_i^k \Rightarrow X_j^k \succcurlyeq X_i^k$, hence $\maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} \subseteq \weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$ and $p_{k,n}^{(F)} \leq q_{k,n}^{(F)}$.

nodes.name: Strong and weak coincide for continuous F
nodes.statement: In particular, when $F$ is continuous, $\maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} = \weakmaxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$, $P$-a.s., hence $p_{k,n}^{(F)}=q_{k,n}^{(F)}$.

nodes.name: All continuous F give the uniform probabilities
nodes.statement: Moreover, let $U(\cdot)$ be the uniform distribution function on $[0,1]$ and observe that every continuous $F$ satisfies the relation \begin{equation} p^{(U)}_{k,n} = p_{k,n}^{(F)} = q_{k,n}^{(F)}=q_{k,n}^{(U)}. \end{equation}
assumptions: let $U(\cdot)$ be the uniform distribution function on $[0,1]$
nodes.statement_short: For continuous $F$, strong and weak maximum probabilities equal those of the uniform distribution.

nodes.name: Bernoulli probability p_{k,n}^{(p)}
nodes.statement: To shorten notation, for every $p\in(0,1)$, let $p_{k,n}^{(p)}$ be the probability of being a maximum once the coordinates have a $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ distribution.

nodes.name: Continuous and Bernoulli are extreme cases
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a general distribution function. Then, \begin{enumerate} \item $p_{k,n}^{(F)} \leq p^{(U)}_{k,n}$. \item $p_{k,n}^{(p)} \leq p_{k,n}^{(F)}$ for every $p \in \left\{1-F(x);x\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $F$ be a general distribution function.
nodes.statement_short: The strong-maximum probability for any $F$ lies between the Bernoulli($p$) value ($p$ in the range of $1-F$) and the continuous value.
nodes.label: prop:weak_strong_different_f

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1 by monotone coupling
nodes.statement: \normalfont $\text{}$ \begin{enumerate} \item The random variables $X_{ij} \sim F$ can be realized by taking uniform random variables $U_{ij} \sim U$, and then taking the transformation $X_{ij} = F^{-1}(U_{ij})$, where $F^{-1}$ is the pseudo-inverse of $F$. Thus, since $F^{-1}$ is nondecreasing we have $U_{j}^k \succcurlyeq U_{i}^k \Rightarrow X_{j}^k \succcurlyeq X_{i}^k $ and hence $X_{i}^k \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} \Rightarrow U_{i}^k \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(U)}$. Therefore, $\maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} \subseteq \maxset{k}{n}^{(U)}$ and hence $p_{k,n}^{(F)} \leq p^{(U)}_{k,n}$. \item Take $x$ with $p \equiv 1-F(x)$ and define $B_{ij} = \textbf{1}_{\{X_{ij} > x\}}$. Since $B_{ij}$ is a nondecreasing transformation of $X_{ij}$, then $B_{i}^j \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(p)} \Rightarrow X_{i}^j \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$. As a result, $\maxset{k}{n}^{(p)} \subseteq \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$ and hence $p_{k,n}^{(p)} \leq p_{k,n}^{(F)}$. \hfill \vrule height1.3ex width1.2ex depth-0.1ex \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Couple via a nondecreasing transformation: $X=F^{-1}(U)$ for the upper bound, $B=\mathbf 1\{X>x\}$ for the lower bound; domination is preserved.

nodes.name: Upper bound via quantile coupling
nodes.statement: The random variables $X_{ij} \sim F$ can be realized by taking uniform random variables $U_{ij} \sim U$, and then taking the transformation $X_{ij} = F^{-1}(U_{ij})$, where $F^{-1}$ is the pseudo-inverse of $F$. Thus, since $F^{-1}$ is nondecreasing we have $U_{j}^k \succcurlyeq U_{i}^k \Rightarrow X_{j}^k \succcurlyeq X_{i}^k $ and hence $X_{i}^k \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} \Rightarrow U_{i}^k \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(U)}$. Therefore, $\maxset{k}{n}^{(F)} \subseteq \maxset{k}{n}^{(U)}$ and hence $p_{k,n}^{(F)} \leq p^{(U)}_{k,n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Realize $X=F^{-1}(U)$; domination of $U$ vectors transfers, so $\mathcal P^{(F)}\subseteq\mathcal P^{(U)}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound via thresholding
nodes.statement: Take $x$ with $p \equiv 1-F(x)$ and define $B_{ij} = \textbf{1}_{\{X_{ij} > x\}}$. Since $B_{ij}$ is a nondecreasing transformation of $X_{ij}$, then $B_{i}^j \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(p)} \Rightarrow X_{i}^j \in \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$. As a result, $\maxset{k}{n}^{(p)} \subseteq \maxset{k}{n}^{(F)}$ and hence $p_{k,n}^{(p)} \leq p_{k,n}^{(F)}$. \hfill \vrule height1.3ex width1.2ex depth-0.1ex
nodes.statement_short: Threshold $B=\mathbf 1\{X>x\}$; maxima of $B$ are maxima of $X$, so $\mathcal P^{(p)}\subseteq\mathcal P^{(F)}$.

nodes.name: No ordering for weak maxima
nodes.statement: \normalfont While $p_{k,n}^{(F)} \leq p^{(U)}_{k,n}$ for any $F$ (i.e. discretization may only reduce the probability of being a {\it strong} maximum), there is no general ordering that always holds between $q_{k,n}^{(F)}$ and $q_{k,n}^{(U)}$. This is demonstrated numerically for the Bernoulli distribution in Section \ref{subsec: numerics}.

nodes.name: Exact formulas for p_{k,n}^{(U)}
nodes.statement: For every $k,n\geq1$, there are well-known exact formulas for $p_{k,n}^{(U)}$ (see e.g. \cite{bai2005maxima}): \begin{enumerate} \item \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(U)} = \sum_{u=1}^n\binom{n-1}{u-1}\frac{(-1)^{u-1}}{u^k}. \end{equation} \item \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(U)}=\begin{dcases} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{u=1}^n p_{k-1,u}^{(U)}, &k>1, \\ \frac{1}{n}, &k=1, \end{dcases} \end{equation} and hence, for every $k>1$ one has \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(U)}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{k,n}} \frac{1}{u_1 u_2 ... u_{k-1}} \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \mathcal{U}_{k,n}\equiv\left\{u=(u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{k-1}\ ;\ 1\leq u_1\leq u_2\leq\ldots\leq u_{k-1}\leq n\right\}. \end{equation} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating-sum formula, a recurrence in $k$, and a sum over nondecreasing integer tuples for the continuous-case probability.

nodes.name: Recurrence for p^{(U)}
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}^{(U)}=\begin{dcases} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{u=1}^n p_{k-1,u}^{(U)}, &k>1, \\ \frac{1}{n}, &k=1, \end{dcases}
nodes.label: eq: recurrence

nodes.name: Sum over nondecreasing tuples
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}^{(U)}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{k,n}} \frac{1}{u_1 u_2 ... u_{k-1}}
nodes.label: eq:sum_u_k_formula

nodes.name: Index set U_{k,n}
nodes.statement: \mathcal{U}_{k,n}\equiv\left\{u=(u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{k-1}\ ;\ 1\leq u_1\leq u_2\leq\ldots\leq u_{k-1}\leq n\right\}.

nodes.name: Fixed-k asymptotics of p_{k,n}^{(U)}
nodes.statement: Furthermore, it is well known (see, e.g., \cite{barndorff1966distribution}) that for every fixed $k$, \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(U)}\sim\frac{\log^{k-1}(n)}{n (k-1)!}\ \ \text{as}\ \ n\to\infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: p^{(U)} ~ log^{k-1}(n)/(n(k-1)!)
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}^{(U)}\sim\frac{\log^{k-1}(n)}{n (k-1)!}\ \ \text{as}\ \ n\to\infty.

nodes.name: Hwang's first-order approximation
nodes.statement: Specifically, let $\Phi(\cdot)$ be the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal random variable, and let $\Gamma(\cdot)$ be the Gamma function. Then, the first order approximation which appears in \cite{hwang2004phase} is \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(U)}\sim\begin{cases} \frac{\log^{k-1}(n)}{n(k-1)!}\Gamma\left[1-\frac{k}{\log(n)}\right], & \log(n)-k\gg\sqrt{\log(n)}, \\ \Phi\left[\frac{k-\log(n)}{\sqrt{\log(n)}}\right], & |k-\log(n)|=o\left[\log^{\frac{2}{3}}(n)\right], \\ 1, & \sqrt{\log(n)}\ll k-\log(n), \end{cases} \end{equation} and it holds uniformly for all variations of $k$ as $n\to\infty$.
assumptions: let $\Phi(\cdot)$ be the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal random variable
conclusions: it holds uniformly for all variations of $k$ as $n\to\infty$
nodes.statement_short: Three-regime approximation of $p^{(U)}_{k,n}$: Gamma-corrected fixed-$k$ formula below, a normal cdf window around, and 1 above $k\approx\log n$.

nodes.name: Hwang 2004 approximation
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}^{(U)}\sim\begin{cases} \frac{\log^{k-1}(n)}{n(k-1)!}\Gamma\left[1-\frac{k}{\log(n)}\right], & \log(n)-k\gg\sqrt{\log(n)}, \\ \Phi\left[\frac{k-\log(n)}{\sqrt{\log(n)}}\right], & |k-\log(n)|=o\left[\log^{\frac{2}{3}}(n)\right], \\ 1, & \sqrt{\log(n)}\ll k-\log(n), \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq: Hwang2004

nodes.name: Hwang's approximation implies Corollary 1 (continuous case)
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma=1$ for every continuous $F$, it may be verified that \eqref{eq: Hwang2004} implies Corollary \ref{cor: main corollary}.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 not straightforward from Hwang
nodes.statement: However, since convergence in $P$ does not imply convergence $P$-a.s., it is not straightforward to deduce Theorem \ref{thm: main result1} from \eqref{eq: Hwang2004}, even for the continuous case.

nodes.name: Hwang's question: probabilistic explanation of the phase transition
nodes.statement: In fact, Hwang \cite{hwang2004phase} put forth the question of whether exists a probabilistic explanation for the phase-transition at $k\approx\log(n)$?

nodes.name: Theorem 1 as a probabilistic explanation
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm: main result1} yields some probabilistic explanation for this phenomenon, although it does not supply a probabilistic proof of \eqref{eq: Hwang2004}.

nodes.name: Exact formula for p_{k,n}^{(p)} (Bernoulli)
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on the number of ones in vector 1 gives $p^{(p)}_{k,n}=\sum_i\binom ki p^i(1-p)^{k-i}(1-p^i)^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli exact formula
nodes.label: eq:binary_p_k_n

nodes.name: Fixed-k asymptotics, Bernoulli strong maximum
nodes.statement: Since $(1 - p^{i})^{n-1} = o\left[(1 - p^{k})^{n-1}\right]$ for all $i<k$ as $n\to\infty$, all terms in the above sum are negligible for large $n$ except for the last, giving the result \begin{equation} p_{k,n}^{(p)} \sim p^{k} (1-p^{k})^{n-1} \ \ \text{as}\ \ n\to\infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: p^{(p)} ~ p^k (1-p^k)^{n-1}
nodes.statement: p_{k,n}^{(p)} \sim p^{k} (1-p^{k})^{n-1} \ \ \text{as}\ \ n\to\infty.

nodes.name: Exact Bernoulli formula hard to analyze
nodes.statement: \normalfont While \eqref{eq:binary_p_k_n} is an exact combinatorial formula for $p^{(p)}_{k,n}$, it is not straightforward to analyze the behaviour of this combinatorial formula as $n\to\infty$ when $k$ is determined as a general function of $n$. Theorem \ref{thm: main result1} gives us the asymptotic result for $p_{k,n}$ as $k,n \to \infty$ without relying on the exact expression.

nodes.name: Exact formula for weak maximum, Bernoulli
conclusions: the asymptotic result $q_{k,n}^{(p)} \to p^{k}$ for fixed $k$ as $n \to \infty$
nodes.statement_short: Analogous conditioning gives an exact sum for $q^{(p)}_{k,n}$, and $q^{(p)}_{k,n}\to p^k$ for fixed $k$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli weak-maximum formula
nodes.label: eq:binary_p_k_n_weak

nodes.name: Contrast of decay rates: continuous vs Bernoulli
nodes.statement: \normalfont For any fixed $k$ the decay of $p^{(U)}_{k,n}=q^{(U)}_{k,n}$ is sub-linear in $n$ as $n \to \infty$ (see \eqref{eq:continuous_fixed_k_asymptotics}). In contrast, $p_{k,n}^{(p)}$ decays to zero exponentially fast, whereas $q_{k,n}^{(p)}$ converges to a positive constant. The result is intuitive because for any fixed $k$ the number of possible vectors in the Bernoulli case is finite, and the vector $(1,..,1)$ (with $k$ coordinates) appears at least once $P$-a.s. as $n \to \infty$. A strong maximum may exist only if this vector appears at most once, an event with an exponentially small probability in $n$. Any occurrence of this vector is a weak maximum, yielding a limit positive probability not depending on $n$, $P\big(X_i^k = (1,..,1)\big)=p^k$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous case decays like $\log^{k-1}n/n$, Bernoulli strong maximum exponentially, weak maximum tends to $p^k$ since $(1,\dots,1)$ appears.

nodes.name: Pair counts B_ij and their multinomial law
nodes.statement: For every $i,j\in\{0,1\}$ define \begin{equation} B_{ij}\equiv\left|\left\{1\leq r\leq k; X_{1r}=i,X_{2r}=j\right\}\right|. \end{equation} and observe that vector $(B_{00}, B_{01}, B_{10}, B_{11})$ has a multinomial distribution, i.e., \begin{equation} (B_{00}, B_{01}, B_{10}, B_{11}) \sim Multinomial\Big(k, \big((1-p)^2, p(1-p), p(1-p), p^2\big)\Big). \end{equation}

nodes.statement: B_{ij}\equiv\left|\left\{1\leq r\leq k; X_{1r}=i,X_{2r}=j\right\}\right|.

nodes.name: Multinomial law of (B_00,...,B_11)

nodes.name: Variance of the Bernoulli Pareto-front size
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on the pair counts gives $P(1,2\in\mathcal P)$ and hence an exact variance of the front size.

nodes.name: Joint probability that vectors 1 and 2 are maxima
Degenerate limit for fixed k
nodes.statement: \normalfont When $k$ is fixed and $n \to \infty$, both the expectation $np_{k,n}^{(p)}$ and variance $V_{k,n}^{(p)}$ approach to zero as $n \to \infty$, hence the limiting distribution of the Pareto-front size is degenerate. An interesting question for future work is whether there exists a sequence $k=k_n$ such that the limiting distribution of the Pareto-front size $|\maxset{k}{n}^{(p)}|$ is non-degenerate.

nodes.statement: An interesting question for future work is whether there exists a sequence $k=k_n$ such that the limiting distribution of the Pareto-front size $|\maxset{k}{n}^{(p)}|$ is non-degenerate.

nodes.name: Other distributions as follow-up
nodes.statement: \normalfont In this part we have analyzed the relatively simple case when the underlying distribution is Bernoulli. Naturally, a follow-up question is about studying other distributions with the goal of comparing between the results.

nodes.name: Numerical comparison Bernoulli vs continuous
nodes.statement: A numerical comparison between the Bernoulli and continuous cases is shown in Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}. The difference in the asymptotic behaviour between $p_{k,n}^{(p)}, q_{k,n}^{(p)}$ and $p^{(U)}_{k,n}(=q^{(U)}_{k,n})$ for fixed $k$ as $n \to \infty$ is shown in Figure 1.a. A numerical demonstration for the different behaviour of $p^{(U)}_{k_n,n}$ for $k_n = c \log(n)$ when $c < 1$ and $c > 1$ is shown in Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}.b. Similarly, the phase transition for $\text{Bernoulli}(0.5)$ is presented in Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}.c, illustrating the localization at $\gamma = \frac{1}{2} \log(2)$, compared to $\gamma=1$ for the continuous case.
nodes.statement_short: Figure 1 shows fixed-$k$ behaviour and the phase transition at $k_n=c\log n$ for uniform and Bernoulli(0.5).

nodes.name: Phase transition also holds for weak maxima
nodes.statement: However, when both $k,n \to \infty$, Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}.c suggests that the phase transition established by Theorem \ref{thm: main result1} for $p_{k,n}^{(p)}$ also holds for $q_{k,n}^{(p)}$.
conclusions: the phase transition established by Theorem \ref{thm: main result1} for $p_{k,n}^{(p)}$ also holds for $q_{k,n}^{(p)}$

nodes.name: Numerical computation method
nodes.statement: For numerical calculation of $p^{(U)}_{k,n}$ we have used the recurrence relation \eqref{eq: recurrence}, because the alternating sum in the combinatorial formula \eqref{eq: combinatorial formula} causes numerical instabilities. As a result, computing $p^{(U)}_{k,n}$ for fixed $k$ requires $O(n)$ operations, and $p^{(U)}_{k.n}$ was calculated for values up to $n=10^7$ in Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}.b. In contrast, the discrete combinatorial formula \eqref{eq:binary_p_k_n} for $p_{k,n}^{(p)}$ can be applied directly, enabling us to compute this probability for much larger values of $n$ (up to $n \approx 10^{130}$) in Figure \ref{fig:discrete_phase_transition}.c. The code for all numeric calculations is freely available at \href{https://github.com/orzuk/Pareto}{https://github.com/orzuk/Pareto}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the recurrence (stable, $O(n)$ per $k$) for the continuous case and the direct Bernoulli formula up to $n\approx10^{130}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Reduce maximality to $M_n^1\le k-1$ for a maximum of dependent geometrics, sandwich $M_n^1$ between maxima of iid geometrics (Lemma 1), and apply Ferguson. Key step: $M_n^1/\log n\to1/\gamma$ a.s.

nodes.name: Reduction to the maximum of dependent geometric variables
nodes.statement_short: Encode maximality through $M_n^1$ and couple it with iid geometric maxima.

nodes.name: Define G_i^1
nodes.statement: For every $i\geq2$, let \begin{equation} G_i^{1}\equiv\min\left\{k\geq1; X_{ik}< X_{1k}\right\}-1. \end{equation} Then $X_1^k\preceq X_i^k$ for every $1\leq k\leq G^{1}_i$ and $X_1^k\not \preceq X_i^k$ for every $k> G^{1}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: $G_i^1$ = length of the initial run on which $X_i$ dominates $X_1$.

nodes.name: G_i^1 definition
nodes.statement: G_i^{1}\equiv\min\left\{k\geq1; X_{ik}< X_{1k}\right\}-1.

nodes.name: Maximality criterion via M_n^1
nodes.statement: In particular, this implies that for every $n,k\geq1$, \begin{equation} 1 \in \maxset{k}{n}\Leftrightarrow M_n^{1}\equiv\max_{2\leq i\leq n} G_i^1\leq k-1 \end{equation} with the convention that a maximum over an empty-set of numbers equals zero.
nodes.statement_short: Vector 1 is a maximum iff $M_n^1=\max_i G_i^1\le k-1$.

nodes.name: Max condition 1 in P_{k,n} iff M_n^1 <= k-1
nodes.statement: 1 \in \maxset{k}{n}\Leftrightarrow M_n^{1}\equiv\max_{2\leq i\leq n} G_i^1\leq k-1
nodes.label: eq: max condition

nodes.name: M_n^1 is a maximum of dependent geometrics
nodes.statement: Thus, the asymptotic behaviour of $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k}{n}}(1)$ as $n,k\to\infty$ is strongly related to the asymptotic behaviour of $M_n^1$ as $n\to\infty$. Observe that $M_n^1$ is a maximum of $n-1$ identically distributed {\it dependent} geometric random variables $G_2^1,G_3^1,\ldots, G_n^1$ having a success probability $P\left(X_{11}>X_{21}\right)$. The following lemma couples $M_n^1$ with a maximum of $n-1$ {\it independent} geometric random variables.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the asymptotics of $M_n^1$, a maximum of identically distributed dependent geometrics.

nodes.name: Coupling lemma and its proof
nodes.statement_short: State and prove Lemma 1 (coupling with iid geometric maxima).

nodes.name: Coupling lemma with iid geometric maxima
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{X_{ij};i,j\geq1\right\}$ be iid random variables with a distribution function $F$ for which $\gamma\equiv\gamma_F$ as defined in \eqref{eq:gamma_def}. In addition, let $G_2,G_3,\ldots$ be an iid sequence of geometric random variables with success probability $\alpha\in(0,1)$. For every $n\geq1$, denote $M_n\equiv M_n^{(\alpha)}\equiv \underset{2\leq i\leq n}{\max} G_i$, and assume that $\left\{G_i ; i\geq2\right\}$ and $\left\{X_{ij};i,j\geq1\right\}$ are independent. Then, for every $\alpha\in(0,1)\setminus\{1-e^{-\gamma}\}$, the random variable \begin{equation} N_\alpha\equiv1+\begin{cases} \sup\left\{n\geq1;M_n>M_n^1\right\}\vee0 & 1-\alpha<e^{-\gamma} \\ \sup\left\{n\geq1;M_n<M_n^1\right\}\vee0 & 1-\alpha>e^{-\gamma} \end{cases} \end{equation} is $P$-a.s. finite.

nodes.name: Summable series, case 2
Continuation: M_n^1/log n -> 1/gamma and conclusion
nodes.statement: It is possible to use Lemma \ref{proposition: basic lemma} in order to show that \begin{equation} \frac{M_n^1}{\log(n)}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\gamma^{-1} , \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} To this end, fix $\epsilon>0$ and let $0<\alpha_1,\alpha_2<1$ be such that \begin{equation*} (1-\alpha_1)e^\gamma<1 < (1-\alpha_2)e^\gamma \end{equation*} and \begin{equation} \left|\gamma^{-1}- \left[\log(1-\alpha_l)\right]^{-1}\right|<\frac{\epsilon}{2} , \ \ \forall l=1,2. \end{equation} Consider two independent iid sequences $G_2^{(\alpha_1)},G_3^{(\alpha_1)},\ldots$ and $G_2^{(\alpha_2)},G_3^{(\alpha_2)},\ldots$ such that $G_1^{(\alpha_l)}\sim\text{Geo}(\alpha_l)$ for $l=1,2$. Respectively, define the corresponding sequences of partial maxima \begin{equation} M_n^{(\alpha_l)}\equiv\max_{2\leq i\leq n}G_i^{(\alpha_l)} , \ \ n\geq2\,, \end{equation} for each $l=1,2$ as described in the statement of Lemma \ref{proposition: basic lemma}. Then, Lemma \ref{proposition: basic lemma} implies that there exists $P$-a.s. finite random variables $N_{\alpha_1}$ and $N_{\alpha_2}$ such that \begin{equation} M_n^{(\alpha_1)}\leq M_n^1\leq M_n^{(\alpha_2)} , \ \ \forall n\geq\max( N_{\alpha_1}, N_{\alpha_2})\equiv N. \end{equation} Furthermore, Theorem $2$ of \cite{Ferguson1993} yields that for each $l=1,2$ \begin{equation} \frac{M_n^{(\alpha_l)}}{\log(n)}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty} - \left[\log(1-\alpha_l)\right]^{-1}\ \ \ , \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} As a result, there exists a $P$-a.s. finite random variable $N^*\geq N$ such that for every $n\geq N^*$ one has \begin{equation} \gamma^{-1}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\leq\frac{M_n^{(\alpha_1)}}{\log (n)}\leq\frac{M_n^1}{\log(n)}\leq\frac{M_n^{(\alpha_2)}}{\log(n)}\leq \gamma^{-1}+\frac{\epsilon}{2} \end{equation} and hence \eqref{eq: extended ferguson} follows. Therefore, \eqref{eq: condition1} implies that \begin{equation} \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n-1}{M_n^1}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}\cdot\frac{k_n-1}{k_{n}}\cdot\frac{\log(n)}{M^1_n}>1, \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} and hence \eqref{eq: max condition} yields that $\textbf{1}_{ \maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}1$, $P$-a.s. Similarly, \eqref{eq: condition2} implies that \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{M_n^1}= \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{k_n}{\log(n)}\cdot\frac{\log(n)}{M^1_n}< 1, \ \ P\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} and hence \eqref{eq: max condition} yields that $\textbf{1}_{\maxset{k_n}{n}}(1)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0$, $P$-a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Show $M_n^1/\log n\to1/\gamma$ a.s. and compare with $k_n$.
